title: 2.7.2 Individual PA Part 2: In Your Own Words
description: Three short-answer questions. Explain the ideas in your own words. AI-graded, summative: one submission, nothing marked on screen.

aiGrader.rubricTitle: Chapter 2 Individual PA, Part 2: In Your Own Words
aiGrader.prompt:
The student answers three short-answer questions in their own words. Mark against the three criteria below. Grade strictly on correctness, generously on phrasing: these are 14-year-olds writing their own words under time pressure. Grammar and spelling are not being assessed. Each criterion is either credited, partially credited, or withheld -- say which in the feedback and why.

Question 1 -- for versus while (worth 4).
The taught distinction (2.4.1): for is the loop whose header carries all three parts -- init, condition, step -- so it fits when you know the range you are walking; while carries only the condition, so it fits when the count is unknown in advance and something inside the body decides when to stop. Credit any answer that gets the when-to-choose reasoning right; the syntax observation (for has three parts in the header, while has one) is supporting detail, not required.

Question 2 -- why the course teaches === and not == (worth 3).
The taught answer (2.1.7, 2.3.18): === compares the value AND the type; == converts before comparing, so 0 == false and "5" == 5 are both true. switch also matches with ===, so a case never matches a value of the wrong type. Credit the coercion explanation and at least one concrete surprise.

Question 3 -- what throw does that console.log does not (worth 3).
The taught answer (2.5.4): throw stops the normal flow and hands the Error to the nearest catch, or ends the program if nothing catches it; console.log prints and the program keeps going. throw is how the program itself reacts to a broken rule; logging is how a human reads about it.

rubric.title: Question 1: when to choose for vs while
rubric.description: Full credit: the response says for suits a known range/count (header packages init, condition, step) while while suits an unknown count decided inside the body. Partial: names one correctly, or describes the syntax difference without the when-to-choose reasoning. Withhold: conflates the two or calls them interchangeable.

rubric.title: Question 2: why === beats ==
rubric.description: Full credit: === compares value and type, == converts first, with at least one concrete surprise (0 == false, or "5" == 5). Partial: coercion named but no example, or an example without the value-and-type distinction. Withhold: says === is better with no reason.

rubric.title: Question 3: throw vs console.log
rubric.description: Full credit: throw stops the flow and hands to the nearest catch (or ends the program uncaught); console.log prints and carries on. Partial: one side explained without the other. Withhold: says throw only crashes the program with no mention of catch.
